items.rawSummary: Internal White House divisions over European troop cuts, hardening stances on Iran and the ICC, and a sharp divergence in U.S. jobs data marked a day of domestic and foreign policy developments, while the Capitol saw a uniformed protest arrest and the revelation of Senator McConnell's medical emergency.
items.analysis: The Pentagon investigation into the Air Force major arrested for a uniformed impeachment protest underscores strict enforcement of political activity rules. Behind the scenes, senior officials including Secretary of State Marco Rubio blocked Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s planned announcement of further U.S. troop cuts in Europe, instead opting for a six-month force posture review amid President Trump’s criticism of NATO spending. On Iran, Trump confirmed that key U.S. demands had been met, but U.S. Ambassador Waltz subsequently warned that presidential patience is not unlimited; Trump later said Iran is 'making no money' and the U.S. will 'take some of the money,' hinting at potential seizure of Iranian assets. The State Department also voiced support for Pakistan's right to self-defense as clashes with Afghanistan continue following their worst fighting in years. Domestically, the White House pushed to deregulate online handgun sales in a move that would benefit a retailer tied to the president’s son, worksite ICE raids surged, and newly released labor market data showed a sharp divergence between payroll and household employment surveys, deepening uncertainty about the labor market alongside a historic drawdown of the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Separately, news emerged that Sen. Mitch McConnell received emergency care for an apparent cardiac arrest, and the Justice Department informed the International Criminal Court that the U.S. rejects its jurisdiction and will not cooperate with investigations.

items.title: Mehrabad Airport, Tehran, Iran: Russian Security Council Deputy Chairman Dmitry Medvedev and a Russian delegation paid their respects at Khamenei's funeral.
items.description: Russian Security Council Deputy Chairman Dmitry Medvedev and a Russian delegation paid their respects at Khamenei's funeral.
items.rawSummary: Funeral ceremonies for Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei in Tehran have drawn over 100 foreign delegations, including Saudi Arabia, Russia, Pakistan, and Lebanon, amid warnings from Iran's parliament speaker about resuming hostilities and ongoing diplomatic and economic overtures.
items.analysis: Funeral ceremonies for Ali Khamenei have begun in Tehran, launching week-long proceedings postponed since February due to war risks, with processions spanning Tehran, Qom, Najaf, and Kerbala and burial set for Thursday in Mashhad. Over 100 foreign delegations are attending, including Lebanon's Defense Minister Michel Mansa alongside Hezbollah and Amal representatives, Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Army Chief Asim Munir, Saudi Deputy Foreign Minister Walid al-Khariji, and Russian Security Council Deputy Chairman Dmitry Medvedev. Top Iranian officials paid respects at the coffin, though newly designated supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei was notably absent. Parliamentary Speaker Ghalibaf warned Iran is prepared to resume military hostilities if frozen assets are not released and the southern Lebanon memorandum not adhered to. Economic and diplomatic moves continue: the Wall Street Journal reported a U.S.-Oman offer to unfreeze some Iranian assets in exchange for no transit fees in the Strait of Hormuz, Qatar agreed to let Iran use $6 billion in frozen funds for goods, and Saudi Arabia transferred five used Boeing 777 wide-body aircraft to Mahan Air, with two confirmed at Mehrabad Airport, despite sanctions. The New York Times disclosed that U.S. officials believed Israel plotted to assassinate Foreign Minister Araghchi and Ghalibaf during spring peace talks, leading to heightened security; at the funeral, authorities reportedly censored identities of visiting Axis of Resistance commanders, and helicopter patrols were visible as the capital remained on high alert.
